facts.claim: "So Long, Honey" is track 4 on Caamp's self-titled debut album, which was released on March 8, 2016.
All songs on the album, including "So Long, Honey", are credited as written by Taylor Meier and Evan Westfall.
The album was produced by Caamp and Jesse Henry, and recorded by Brad Denson, Jason Joyal and Brandon MacLean.
Credits list Brandon MacLean and Jason Joyal as mixers and Brian Lucey as mastering engineer. Sally Taylor Meier is credited with the cover design.
Evan Westfall has described the debut as recorded in an unusual way. Their mentor Jesse Henry, who had been Taylor Meier's guitar teacher, put them in touch with a man named Brad.
Westfall said the album contains hidden references to nicknames and friends the band ran around with, and that these were a big inspiration for it.
Westfall said that on the first album the two wrote sitting across from each other, or Meier brought in a mostly finished song such as "Vagabond" and Westfall then added banjo parts.
Relix describes the 2016 debut as sparse, self-produced and self-titled.
The debut was originally released on Square Roots Records. Its later vinyl pressings carry the catalog number CAAMP001 on Caamp's own label.
Caamp is an indie-folk band from Columbus, Ohio, formed by Taylor Meier (lead vocals, guitar) and Evan Westfall (banjo, harmony vocals, guitar). Bassist Matt Vinson later joined them.

research.lineage: Caamp is an Ohio indie-folk act, built around guitar and banjo with harmonies, that grew out of the Athens, Ohio, coffee-shop and live scene around Ohio University.

draft:
The title reads like a goodbye, but the chorus says otherwise. In **So Long, Honey**, "so long" is about time, not farewell: you can only drift on the wind for so long before you come back down. The narrator isn't seeing anyone off. He's settling in to wait, and the whole song lives in that gap between letting go and refusing to.

Taylor Meier and Evan Westfall wrote it for Caamp's self-titled 2016 debut, a record Relix called sparse and self-produced. Westfall has said the two wrote those early songs sitting across from each other, and you can hear that table-for-two closeness here. The fingerpicked acoustic guitar is bright and clear. The banjo works under it rather than on top. The bass keeps things simple, and the drums hold a relaxed, slightly swung mid-tempo with the snare landing on two and four. The room is dry and close, the take raw at the edges. Meier sings in a slightly raspy mid-range, conversational more than showy, as if he's talking someone down rather than performing for them.

The opening verse sets up the picture the song keeps returning to. Throw a rock and something breaks. Throw a feather and the wind takes it. The person he loves is the feather, and the narrator knows better than to try catching it. That's why the chorus lands so gently: "And when you do, I'll be hangin' around." It's a casual phrase carrying a lot of weight, patience dressed up as loitering, so the want doesn't sound like need.

The second verse drops that guard. There's smoke in the room and a piano that doesn't work, and then a dry little correction: "It never did." Nothing in this place was ever quite in tune. Right after that comes a plain admission, the feeling he gets when this person walks in and the wish that they'd stay. Pride and longing sit side by side, and the song never makes him pick one.

Then it turns outward. The last section drops the lover entirely and becomes a blessing for everyone else: "Be good to your mothers," because they did the best they could, and bleed for your brothers, because they'd do the same for you. Westfall has said the album is full of hidden nods to the friends and nicknames of the crowd the band ran with, and this coda sounds like a toast to that crowd. The "Lord knows" gives it a churchy lift, and the wordless oohs carry it out. The heartbreak doesn't get resolved. It gets folded into a bigger loyalty.

That's the move that sticks: a song about waiting for one person ends by telling you who will still be there while you wait.
